rationale: A wins because it keeps the story honest where the facts are thin. Its line, "24,000 paid teams, 220 million users — and Canva can't name one enterprise customer," is the kind of uncomfortable framing a real business reporter could use; B's "220 million users already inside companies" smuggles in a fact the update does not give. B has usable bones, but it keeps rounding assumptions upward until the launch looks more proven than it is.
gaps_in_A: "The acquisition and the AI generation feature land together" overstates timing; the update says Canva recently acquired an AI image-generation startup, not that the acquisition and feature landed together.
"category-creation" is a bit grand for one constrained-generation product claim without customer evidence or technical proof.
The next step of "newsjack-detector" is defensible, but for launch angles with known holes, customer proof and acquisition details may be more urgent than hunting an external peg.
gaps_in_B: "220 million users already inside companies" is invented. The update says over 220 million monthly users, not that they are inside enterprise accounts.

"competing directly with Adobe Creative Cloud Enterprise and Microsoft 365 for IT budget approval" outruns the facts; the update says Canva is pushing into Adobe and Microsoft territory, not that direct budget displacement is proven.
"Notion, Figma, and Miro ran the same arc" imports outside examples not supplied in the update. That may be true context, but this exercise asked for grounding in the given facts.
"the legal team can make a slide deck without asking design" is a cute imagined use case, not a fact. B later asks for examples, which exposes the headline as decoration.
